open_obligations: Read p14 L47-51 to check whether the authors say their absolute accuracies are not comparable to Parrish et al.'s
Check that Parrish et al.'s two-turn judges had time-limited passage access, unlike Michael et al.'s judges
Compare the baselines: Parrish et al. compare with a no-argument condition; check whether Michael et al. compare with consultancy
out.other_title: Two-turn debate with counter-arguments did not help humans on the authors' reading comprehension task
out.rationale: Parrish et al.'s two-turn study (one argument plus one counter-argument) reports that humans perform similarly with or without arguments. Michael et al. note that in Parrish et al.'s experiments debate does not significantly improve judge accuracy and point to differences between the settings, first that their own debates are unbounded in length, which they suggest may have produced more useful and informative arguments, so the challenge is scoped to protocol.
out.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: Whether multi-turn debate improves human judge accuracy on hard QuALITY questions; the contrast depends on protocol differences, first debate length (unbounded in Michael et al., bounded at a single refutation in Parrish et al.)

text: The authors note that in Parrish et al.'s one- and two-turn debate experiments on QuALITY, debate did not significantly improve judge accuracy, and they point to differences from their own setting. The first is that their debates are unbounded in length rather than limited to a single refutation, which the authors suggest may produce more useful and informative arguments.
title: Unbounded-length debates differ from Parrish et al.'s one- and two-turn QuALITY setting
